title: Local Classes in C++ - GeeksforGeeks
content:
A local class is a class declared inside a function. It is visible only within the function in which it is declared and is commonly used when a class is required only for a specific function.

  • Accessible only within its enclosing function.
  • Helps keep implementation details local and avoids unnecessary global classes.

Example: The following program demonstrates creating a local class inside a function.

CPP 
#include <iostream> 
using namespace std; 
void fun() 
{ 
    class Test { 
    public: 
        void display() 
        { 
            cout << "Local Class"; 
            
        } 
        
    }; 
    
    Test t; 
    t.display(); 
    
} 

int main() 
{ 
    fun(); 
    return 0; 
    
}

Output
Local Class

Explanation

  • Test is declared inside the function fun().
  • The class is visible only inside fun().
  • An object of Test is created and used within the same function.

Syntax

void functionName() {

class ClassName {

// class members

};

ClassName obj;

}

Characteristics of Local Classes

Local classes have several rules that distinguish them from regular classes.

Scope of a Local Class

The name of a local class is visible only inside the function where it is declared.

  • Objects of the class can only be created inside the enclosing function.
  • The class name cannot be used outside the function.

Example: The following program shows that a local class can only be used inside its enclosing function.

CPP 
#include <iostream>
using namespace std;

void fun()
{
    // Local class
    class Test {
        // Body
    };

    Test t; // Fine
    Test* tp; // Fine
}

int main()
{
    Test t; // Error
    Test* tp; // Error
    return 0;
}

Explanation: Test is declared inside fun(), so its scope is limited to that function. Attempting to create an object of Test outside fun() results in a compilation error.

Member Function Definition

All member functions of a local class must be defined inside the class definition.

  • Member functions cannot be defined outside the local class.
  • Defining them outside the class results in a compilation error.

Example (Valid): The following program demonstrates a local class with all member functions defined inside the class.

CPP 
#include <iostream>
using namespace std;

void fun()
{
    class Test // local to fun
    {
    public:
        // Fine as the method is defined
        // inside the local class
        void method()
        {
            cout << "Local Class method() called";
        }
    };

    Test t;
    t.method();
}

int main()
{
    fun();
    return 0;
}

Output
Local Class method() called

Example (Invalid): The following program demonstrates a compilation error caused by defining a local class member function outside the class.

CPP 
#include <iostream>
using namespace std;

void fun()
{
    class Test // local to fun
    {
    public:
        void method();
    };

    // Error as the method is defined outside the local
    // class
    void Test::method() { cout << "Local Class method()"; }
}

int main() { return 0; }

Output 

Compiler Error:
 In function 'void fun()':
 error: a function-definition is not allowed here before '{' token

Static Members

Local classes have restrictions on static members.

  • Static data members are not allowed.
  • Static member functions are allowed.

Example (Invalid): The following program attempts to declare a static data member in a local class, resulting in a compilation error.

CPP 
#include <iostream>
using namespace std;

void fun()
{
    class Test // local to fun
    {
        static int i;
    };
}

int main() { return 0; }

Output

Compiler Error:
 In function 'void fun()':
 error: local class 'class fun()::Test' shall not have static data member 'int fun()::Test::i'

Example (Valid): The following program demonstrates that a local class can contain static member functions.

CPP 
#include <iostream>
using namespace std;

void fun()
{
    class Test // local to fun
    {
    public:
        static void method()
        {
            cout << "Local Class method() called";
        }
    };

    Test::method();
}

int main()
{
    fun();
    return 0;
}

Output
Local Class method() called

Accessing Variables of the Enclosing Function

Member functions of a local class have limited access to variables declared in the enclosing function.

  • Static variables can be accessed.
  • Enumeration constants can be accessed.
  • Non-static local variables cannot be accessed directly.

Example (Valid): The following program demonstrates accessing static and enumeration variables from a local class.

CPP 
#include <iostream>
using namespace std;

void fun()
{
    static int x;
    enum { i = 1, j = 2 };

    // Local class
    class Test {
    public:
        void method()
        {
            cout << "x = " << x
                 << endl; // fine as x is static
            cout << "i = " << i
                 << endl; // fine as i is enum
        }
    };

    Test t;
    t.method();
}

int main()
{
    fun();
    return 0;
}

Output
x = 0
i = 1

Example (Invalid): The following program demonstrates a compilation error caused by accessing a non-static local variable of the enclosing function from a local class.

CPP 
#include <iostream>
using namespace std;

void fun()
{
    int x;

    // Local class
    class Test {
    public:
        void method() { cout << "x = " << x << endl; }
    };

    Test t;
    t.method();
}

int main()
{
    fun();
    return 0;
}

Output

Compiler Error: use of local variable with automatic storage from containing function

Accessing Global Entities 

Local classes can access entities outside the enclosing function.

  • Global variables and functions can be accessed.
  • Global types can be used.
  • Other local classes declared within the same function can also be accessed.

Example: The following program demonstrates accessing global entities and another local class from within a local class.

CPP 
#include <iostream>
using namespace std;

int x;

void fun()
{

    // First Local class
    class Test1 {
    public:
        Test1() { cout << "Test1::Test1()" << endl; }
    };

    // Second Local class
    class Test2 {
        // Fine: A local class can use other local classes
        // of same function
        Test1 t1;

    public:
        void method()
        {
            // Fine: Local class member methods can access
            // global variables.
            cout << "x = " << x << endl;
        }
    };

    Test2 t;
    t.method();
}

int main()
{
    fun();
    return 0;
}

Output
Test1::Test1()
x = 0

Explanation

  • Test2 uses another local class Test1.
  • The local class accesses the global variable x.
  • Local classes can interact with global entities just like regular classes.

Limitations of Local Classes

Local classes have several restrictions compared to regular classes.

  • Can only be used within the enclosing function.
  • Member functions must be defined inside the class.
  • Static data members are not allowed.
  • Cannot directly access non-static local variables of the enclosing function.
